response.title: Is a projector screen that rises up from the floor worth the money over a fixed frame screen, and do they get wrinkles?
response.answer:
A floor-rising projector screen is worth the extra money primarily for aesthetics and convenience, not picture quality. If you have a dedicated home theater, I'd almost always recommend a fixed-frame screen. But if you're putting a projector in a living room and don't want a giant screen permanently on the wall, a floor-rising screen can be worth the premium.

And yes, floor-rising screens can develop wrinkles or waves, even expensive ones. However, the design makes a big difference.

Do floor-rising screens get wrinkles?

There are three main things to watch for.

1. Waves and ripples

Flexible screen material can develop slight waves from changes in temperature, humidity, or uneven tension. These can distort straight lines during projection.

Shop

2. Edge curling

The edges can curl inward over time. Tab-tensioned screens use cables along the sides to help keep the material flat.

Shop

3. Long-term stretching

Repeated raising and lowering, uneven tension, or aging material can contribute to deformation. A well-engineered tensioning system reduces the risk but doesn't eliminate it.

Important: A tab-tensioned floor-rising screen is substantially preferable to a non-tensioned one if you're concerned about wrinkles. But even a good tab-tensioned screen generally cannot match the long-term flatness of a properly installed fixed-frame screen.

How much does the wrinkle risk matter?

It depends heavily on your projector.

Ultra-short-throw (UST) projector: Very important. Even small waves can create noticeable geometric distortion because light hits the screen at such a steep angle.

Standard-throw projector: Less important. Minor waves may be practically invisible during movies, although they can still affect image uniformity.

Independent screen testing confirms that fixed-frame screens generally offer more consistent tension, while tab-tensioning is particularly important for UST projectors. 
The Hook Up
+1

One less obvious concern is that retractable screens can develop permanent pressure marks if dirt gets rolled into the screen material. 
The Hook Up

My recommendation

I'd choose a fixed-frame screen unless hiding the screen is a major priority. With the same budget, you can often get a better screen surface, better flatness, and fewer reliability concerns.

If you do choose floor-rising, prioritize side tensioning, a strong warranty, and a return policy that covers visible waves or distortion. Also check whether the manufacturer requires the screen to extend to its full designed height to maintain tension.

Two questions would help me make a more specific recommendation:

Are you using an ultra-short-throw (UST) projector or a regular projector?

What screen size are you considering — 100", 120", 135", or larger?

These two factors make a surprisingly big difference in whether floor-rising is a good investment.
